speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee.
Last year Japan replaced Great Britain as the biggest commercial importer of wheat in the world. As of last March 31 Japan had bought abroad 4.2 million tons of wheat. Last year Canada enjoyed 30.4 per cent of that huge market. The United States had 55.8 per cent and Australia had 13.8 per cent. But today both France and Argentina have cut themselves a big slice of the Japanese market. There are now five sellers where there used to be three. They used to be frozen out, but now they are in strong. It is plain they did this by price cutting, but the fact remains that they did it. They made sales and we did not.
It looks as though the two newcomers are in the Japanese wheat market to stay. The Japanese want it that way. They have adopted a national policy of acquiring a diversity of overseas suppliers, not only in respect of wheat but in respect of other products such as minerals and other raw materials. The Japanese have learned in recent years that they can get the best wheat for the best price if they shop for it. Canada's old, steady and easy markets are gone forever. That is the single most important fact of today's world of wheat.
We are living in a world that has changed from 1966. The market has changed; tastes abroad have changed and the demands of old customers have changed. Unless we get with this change we will be left at the post. My suggestion to the Prime Minister and to the Ministers of Agriculture and Industry, Trade and Commerce is to treat this as an emergency. They should convene a special meeting to consider appropriate measures, whether they be subsidies, price-cutting, more generous credit terms or a combination of all these possible expedients. The vital thing is fast and decisive action.
I have no doubt from the way the minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce spoke a few weeks ago that he hopes to dazzle the house one day soon with an announcement of foreign sales of wheat. The Canadian wheat producer is not interested in any flash in the pan sale but in an assurance that major hurdles to marketing have been overcome.
Reference has been made recently to the fact that the task force has suggested, as one alternative to the overproduction of grain, that we eliminate 33J per cent or about 4 of our wheat acreage in western Canada. This would amount to something like 10 million acres. I do not have to ask many questions or make many remarks to precipitate in the minds of hon. members the question as to what will be the alternative income of farmers in western Canada if we eliminate 10 million acres of wheat producing land in western Canada. I hope this is not going to be the policy of the government.
The other alternative suggested is that farmers get into feed grain production. We have a surplus of feed grain at the present time. If everyone got into the production of feed grain I wonder what would happen to that market. The wheat producers want assurance of massive and continuing sales in order that they will have some measure of stability and prosperity. If there is not some evidence that Canada has modernized her wheat marketing techniques, the Canadian wheat producer will be driven from the field and a large and valuable part of the Canadian economy will have been irretrievably damaged. Let us have more action and fewer promises from the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I shall speak for only a few minutes because I am told that the house would like to pass this evening that section of the bill that deals with

March 12, 1969	COMMONS
the establishment of a Department of Supply
and Services.
I shall therefore comment briefly on some of the remarks made by my hon. colleagues. First of all, the members from Prince Edward-Hastings and Waterloo (Messrs. Hees and Saltsman) seem to hold diametrically opposed stands. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings claims that the Department of Industry should never have existed, that it represented a total loss of $50 million.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Waterloo tells us that the Department of Industry should continue to exist as an independent department, because as separate from the Department of Trade and Commerce it is in a better position to contribute to industrial development. Contrary to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings, he blames us for not having spent enough in that field.
The two members therefore give the impression of being diametrically opposed to each other, but they are not, for they both ignore the same things. They ignore what the Department of Industry did since 1963-and this applies particularly to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings-and what it will continue to do. This applies also to the hon. member for Waterloo. It will do more, and better, because of the fact of its coexistence, of its amalgamation with the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Therefore, although seemingly opposed, in fact the two hon. members have a point in common in that they ignore the same things.
I wish I had more time to point out today once more what the Department of Agriculture has done since 1963, recall the programs it enacted, and their carrying into effect but obviously my time is running short. However, I want to point out two factors, two things that the Department of Industry has accomplished: First, that Department has acquired an excellent knowledge of the existing Canadian industry, and has compiled data on each industrial sector.
Studies were made-some were mentioned earlier-on the chemical industry, the dairy industry, and so forth, and these studies are now the extremely useful source of data for government policy making.
I would also like to say a few words about the importance of co-operation between federal departments and industry, and in this respect also the Department of Industry has done a great deal, as I said yesterday, to
DEBATES	6551
Government Organization strengthen co-operation between the government and industrial sectors.
There are for example, in various fields such as textiles, footwear, chemicals, plastics, etc., advisory committees which meet regularly and analyse the different situations. Once again, they represent an excellent source of information for the government.
I took part in a certain number of these meetings. One could gain some fringe benefits from those meetings. Very often, representatives of the private sector who attended the meetings had the chance of meeting one another, an opportunity which apparently they seldom had.
And very often, at a meeting with representatives of the government, the industrialists themselves would profit from these meetings. I could also talk of the new advisory committee which met recently. I could talk of the export committees, about sixty in number, which exist today. My objective would be to show the contribution the Department of Industry in bringing closer together the government and industrial sectors, one of its greatest achievements.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

The hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour gave us a few items of his good philosophy. He told us about the tremendous potentiality of the west. I am aware of that potentiality having been the minister responsible for things like oil, gas, coal and water in my previous capacity, and as the minister now responsible for wheat I am very much aware of the tremendous importance of the western economy in our national economy. He told us about the need for freer trade with the United States in particular. I would like the hon. member to read tomorrow the following quotation from my notes: "The United States agreed-this is under the Kennedy round-to significantly reduce tariffs on more than $2 billion of Canadian exports in 1966 terms. The bulk of Canadian exports of foodstuffs and industrial materials to the United States will face very low tariffs or free entry. When the final reductions are made, over 60 per cent of our total current sales to the United States will be duty free."
That will be of comfort to the hon. member.

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
This tremendous B.C. aggressiveness and intelligence will have ample occasion to demonstrate itself on U.S. markets,


Government Organization California included. The hon. member also made the suggestion that we should very soon send a mission to the Pacific rim. I am looking into that. But as a "cash advance payment" I might use this occasion to say that I will be going to some countries of the Pacific after the Japan-Canada ministerial meeting in April. I suppose that a two-man mission, my deputy minister is also coming, is not as good as the kind of mission the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour had in mind, but this should be an indication of our interest in the Pacific as a trading area.
I had some intelligent comment to make at this point on the fact that it is very difficult for the Canadian government, in answering the numerous requests that are made on it, to establish priorities in trade matters. The moment somebody says that Latin-America is very important and the government agrees that a mission be sent there, somebody else mentions the tremendous importance of the Pacific rim and we all agree that we could send a mission there too. Somebody the other day was telling me that Germany is so tremendously rich that obviously we should have a mission there. The West Indies are very important also for us, and we should not neglect Europe or the United Kingdom which is still a very important market. And eastern Europe is also very, very important. China, obviously, is extremely important, and Russia should not be neglected either. Consequently, where do we go first? I think the conclusion might now be drawn that Canada is one of those countries which has an interest all over the world and consequently should be present everywhere. This does not solve the question of establishing priorities.

The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard) and the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) said most interesting things about the textile industry. I can confirm that the study referred to is going on at present. It is an attempt to identify the sectors of the textile industry that are profitable, quite so, in order to promote their further growth and make them even more profitable. The study is also designed, unfortunately, to identify a number of sectors that are less profitable, and then, this is the problem: what are we to do with those sectors?
As far as I am concerned, I find the industrial readjustment principle contained in the automobile agreement and contained as well in the Kennedy Round agreements extremely sensible and human. The purpose of that

study is precisely to determine whether it is possible to think in those terms also with regard to the less profitable sectors of the textile industry.
I hesitate to deal with those matters, because there are so many things to be said. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres mentioned a number of them in reply to the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe who had assumed that I knew all about it. One of the things that should be said is that even though governments are quite willing to take a human attitude toward the problems of industries, it might be detrimental to them to maintain plants and industries unable to survive and to prosper. Very often, it is a bad service to render an unsound industry to give it millions of dollars in order to deteriorate further or more decently, when we know full well that any day, it will have to close down and that other factors than imports play a very important role in the plight of some industries. I took the member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), to task earlier, because he did not emphasize enough the fact that imports are not the only factor responsible for the plight of a number of plants but that in many cases, those plants have not been modernized, do not have the kind of management they should have, because if they were well managed, they would not be in such a predicament.
As I said earlier. I would need much more time to look into every aspect of those problems.

speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, there were changes everywhere, which only proves that progress is with us.
I would have a few words to say also to the member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) who spoke in defence of the small industry. While listening to him, I happened to think that the kind of help he wanted us to give industry was likely to turn it into big industry. And then, of course, he would be the first to think that we are helping too much that big industry. This type of remarks is due perhaps to my somewhat strange character.
My department makes all its services available to the small industry and I could give a list of several things we can do for it. But there is no doubt that it is largely the big
March 12. 1969	COMMONS
industry which takes advantage of my department's services.
As the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) said, small industries are often located in underdeveloped areas. There is no doubt that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will apply itself more directly than mine to the problems of at least some of those small businesses.
I might even say that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is especially-I do not say exclusively-responsible for the big industry, so that the government can get, through taxation, the money necessary to deal with underdeveloped areas.
The hon. member also mentioned the dangers or the negative effects of modernization. What I said earlier about the need for industrial rehabilitation applies. As there is retraining for individuals, there should also be some kind of retraining for industries.
The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) is very concerned about the bilingual character of my department. I can assure him that most people mentioned: Messrs. Warren, Kniewasser, Scharzmann, Senecal and Mundy, are all bilingual. In fact, I am proud to have a department that can work, at least at the upper level in both languages. Therefore, I can reassure the hon. member and all other French-speaking members in the house that if they have to deal with those senior officials, they can start the conversation in French and carry on in French.
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) has raised a question which I find most interesting, to wit the confidential nature of certain government papers. That is, I believe, a controversial matter in the sense that certain papers may readily be made public while the same is not true of others.
I have here a list of the studies done by the department. Some have been made known to the organizations with which they had been undertaken, while others, for obvious reasons, were not distributed. Some interests are involved and even if we are democratically minded, such interest must be protected when, for example, publication of a document may cause economic disturbances which would not be in the best interests of the country.
I suggest that we must be practical, that we must distinguish between the two kinds and that we must act accordingly.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam) has given us the background of the wheat situation. I simply
DEBATES	6553
Government Organization envy him for having been able to prepare a historical outline as complete as the one he has offered us this afternoon. I would have preferred him to tell me what to do tomorrow. In any event, there will certainly be an opportunity for me tomorrow to tell what I intend to do.
I would like to take perhaps three minutes to answer the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) who brought up a discussion which we had started a few months ago and which, so far as I am concerned, interests me, and even grips my heart.

We could argue the case on financial grounds. We can ask whether one company can get more from civilian programs than from the defence programs of the department. What I said a few months ago in the house, and I quote it, is that "the Canadian industrialists who avail themselves of our programs might get as much from a civilian project as from a defence project". I still maintain that this is possible, and we will have an opportunity, when we study my estimates in the committee, to get down to details and to show that this is true.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
However, I do not think that this is the essential difference between the point of view of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and my own. The real difference is on general ideas. I sympathize with parts of his philosophy, as I have said before. I am in favour also of a shift from the defence aspect to the civilian aspect, inasmuch as this is possible and this is done, too. I am as peaceful as he is, and sometimes perhaps more peaceful than he, at least in my approach to political matters. However, the difference between us is really more basic than that and I wish I had time to go into it. The basic difference is probably in our approach to defence and to foreign affairs. The real debate would consist in asking what form and what degree of involvement Canada should have in world affairs. We would have to start with this basic question in order to come to some kind of conclusion. Then, I would have to say many things about the purpose of the defence programs in my department. May I mention a few, en passant. The first is that the defence program is designed to give the best value for the Canadian defence dollar. However, if my hon. friend does not want Canada to spend any money on defence, that brings about an altogether different debate, as I have said. I


Government Organization assume in my argumentation that there is a need for Canadian defence equipment and that we should not have to buy all our defence material outside of Canada, most probably in the United States, and in this way emphasize our dependence, if it can be called that, on the United States.
The moment you say that Canada must have a defence program, you are confronted with a choice: Will you buy all the military equipment from outside Canada, will you make it here or will you do some of both. If you are going to have a defence program it would be silly not to take advantage of our own industrial capacity. The hon. member can see how basic the debate between us would be if we had time to go into it.

speechtext: May I assume the minister would permit me to ask him a question? I was not sure whether he was implying that I was suggesting we had no defence need and therefore should scrap all our military purchases. I did not say that. I assume we have a defence requirement. Would the minister also agree that a study was done by his department which reached the conclusion that strictly on economic terms it would be advantageous for us to purchase the major part of our military equipment abroad in the competitive market?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
The matter is still more basic than that. I am thinking of the industrial development and of the advantages of a defence industry program.
I would like to say one more word on this subject. What can be classed as offensive equipment which Canada sells abroad? My officials say that it can be brought down to 10 per cent. A plane can be used for civilian purposes as well as military purposes. Are you going to exclude everything that could have a military implication? If so, I say you are in trouble. Already we have 15,000 Canadians working in this industry, and if you want to be categorical about these things, you will be in great trouble. I am sure the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby would be the last one to say that we should not export materials, minerals, or anything else that would have a military application. There is no end to the potential list. We then come to the question of who is the aggressor and who is not the aggressor, how do you define aggression,
what is a defensive instrument, and what is an offensive weapon. These are philosophical debates which were very popular in the middle ages but I was hoping we would not get involved in them here tonight.
However, I love a challenge, and if the hon. member would like to debate these matters, I am ready to accept his invitation. I am afraid I do not have the time to find a platform; I leave that to him.
Clause agreed to.
